newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS--France seeks to lift optimism with tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--France seeks to lift optimism with tax cuts.

text.p: France's conservative government, battling weak growth and high unemployment, announced on Thursday cuts in income tax designed to snap the country out of its mood of pessism.

"By cutting taxes, we are giving extra purchasing power to those who are hesitating to spend, or buy new goods because the tax burden they face is too high," Prime Minister Alain Juppe said in a television address to the nation.

Officials have said the aim is to lift consumer spending, stalled by fears about record unemployment, and underpin an economic recovery that is meant to take France smoothly into European monetary union before the end of the century.

The government said in a statement that it would cut income taxes by 75 billion francs over the next five years, reduce all income tax rates, bringing the top rate of tax eventually down to 47 percent from 56.8 and increase the threshold before people start paying tax to help those on low incomes.

It said it would cut income taxes by 25 billion francs next year, although part of that will be recouped through heavier taxation elsewhere, particularly on savings, to pay for the deficit-burdened welfare system.
As a result the net tax cut next year will be 18 billion francs, the government said in a statement.
The government also shifted taxes off the cost of labour, cutting payroll charges for healthcare by 1.3 percentage points, in a bid to encourage employment.

But it said it was raising the CSG (Generalised Social Contribution), used to finance welfare spending, to 3.4 percent from 2.4 percent and would in future apply it to a wider range of income, hitting savings.

In a radical overhaul bound to provoke ire in many corners, it also said it was tightening up on tax breaks on contributions to new life assurance policies immediately and scrapping special tax deductions for some 100 professions from 1998.

The government will also introduce independently managed pension funds to complement the existing system of universal pensions, a plan long questioned by some opposition politicians who fear an erosion of France's generous welfare state.

In announcing the tax cuts -- only a day after news that the economy shrank in the second quarter -- Juppe appeared to be seeking to maximise the psychological impact of good news ahead of a tough spending-cutting budget due later this month.

In reality the tax cuts next year are not that large -- and far less than some 60 billion francs in spending cuts expected in the 1997 budget. Their benefit to consumers may be reduced even further by the 1997 budget, which is expected to increase excise duties, particularly on alcohol and tobacco.

But Juppe, who has pledged to reduce France's public sector deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from five percent last year to meet European monetary union entry requirements, has little room for manoeuvre.
At best he can hope for a "feel-good" factor, encouraging consumption -- and the government's popularity ahead of 1998 parliamentary elections.

"The global policy will be a tight fiscal policy. You cannot expect to boost growth when you really have to cut the budget deficit which is the situation in this country," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said.

The opposition Socialist party slammed the new measures, complaining that Juppe had already raised Value Added Tax, a sales tax paid by everyone, whereas now he was lowering income tax, paid only by those who earned enough to pay it.

"This measure is utterly unjust," Socialist spokesman Dominique Strauss-Kahn said. "It could even worsen recession if people choose to save the money they they don't give the tax man, while on the other hand public spending falls."
